newsitem.title: USA: NASA says weather good for Sunday shuttle launch.
newsitem.headline: NASA says weather good for Sunday shuttle launch.

text.p: The countdown continued on Friday for the weekend blastoff of the space shuttle Atlantis on a mission to Russia's Mir station, but the loss of a U.S. weather satellite was affecting the accuracy of NASA's weather forecast for launch, officials said.
U.S. Air Force forecasters were predicting cold but favourable conditions for Sunday morning's planned pre-dawn blastoff from Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.

But the unexpected shutdown of the GOES-8 weather satellite, which covers the U.S. East Coast, has forced meteorologists to rely on a West Coast satellite that cannot take overhead views of the Florida launch site.
"It's not optimum for us," shuttle weather officer Ed Priselac said. "Your resolution is much poorer."
Forecasters would monitor the weather during Sunday's launch attempt with information from aircraft and ground-based monitoring stations, he said.

Priselac gave the shuttle a 70 percent chance of launching during its short seven-minute launch window, which opens at 4:27 a.m. EST (0927 GMT). Weather conditions were expected to deteriorate on Monday and Tuesday.
"Both days do not look promising," he said. "So we would like to go for Sunday."
If the launch was delayed beyond Tuesday, the shuttle would have to wait until after an unmanned Delta rocket was launched from neighbouring Cape Canaveral Air Station.
Atlantis was to pick up U.S. astronaut John Blaha from the Mir station and drop off his replacement, Jerry Linenger, for a four-month stay.
Blaha, who has been aboard the station since September, told Cable News Network on Thursday he had missed his wife of 30 years, Brenda, and was ready to come home.
"That's what I've missed the most, my wife," Blaha said. "I had no idea, I must say, how I would feel about the separation from her."
The shuttle was also to deliver about 3,600 lbs (1,600 kg) of food and supplies for the orbiting space outpost.
Elsewhere at the sprawling Florida launch site, technicians were trying to determine if a fire has damaged a space laboratory due for launch aboard shuttle Columbia in March.
A power supply close to the laboratory module caught fire on Thursday, filling an ultra-clean space centre hangar with smoke, NASA spokesman George Diller said.

Although the fire was quickly brought under control, there was concern about possible smoke damage to the laboratory. NASA officials expected to know on Monday if the laboratory's electronics and science experiments were affected.
